title: Trio of galaxies mixes it up
caption: The galaxy group Hickson Compact Group 90, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HCG 90, NGC 7173, NGC 7174, NGC 7176 · constellation Piscis Austrinus · about 120 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA and R. Sharples (University of Durham, U.K.)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Three galaxies share this Hubble view, with NGC 7173 at middle left, NGC 7174 at middle right and NGC 7176 at lower right. They belong to Hickson Compact Group 90, about 120 million light-years away in Piscis Austrinus, named after the astronomer Paul Hickson, who first cataloged compact groups like this one during the 1980s.

NGC 7173 and NGC 7176 look like smooth, ordinary elliptical galaxies without much gas or dust. An elliptical galaxy is a rounded collection of stars with little of the raw material that fuels new star formation. NGC 7174 is very different, a mangled spiral barely holding on as a separate galaxy while its close neighbors tear it apart.

The strong tidal forces running through the group have pulled large numbers of stars away from their home galaxies. Those stars are now spread thinly, forming a faint, glowing component that belongs to the group as a whole rather than to any one galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.25 x 3.25 arcminutes) and distance (120 million light years), the frame spans roughly 113,000 × 113,000 light-years. Its light set out about 120 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal the faint glow of scattered stars that the eye would miss.
